title: Gold for Palestine: Karate's Mariam Bsharat a rare sporting success
summary: The occupied West Bank is not an obvious breeding ground for sporting success. But Mariam Bsharat, 17, has beaten the odds to become a karate world champion and is making a new life in Germany.

image.caption: Mariam Bsharat has won back to back world titles in karateImage: Fabienne Abu Wahib/Karate Insights/PS Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: "After the referee lifted my hand to show I'm now a two-time world champion, it was a very overwhelming feeling. Making history once is something, but making it twice is really something else. I felt very happy and I felt a big relief. Only I know how many sacrifices I made and how many hardships I needed to overcome."

Themes of relief, joy and sacrifice are commonplace in the reflections of athletes after a big win. But in Mariam Bsharat's case, it's about more than just dedication to training and taking care of the body. The karate athlete, 17, won a second under-21 World Championship gold medal in Poland earlier this month competing for her native Palestine.
"It was everyday life, seeing people get killed around me and houses getting bombed," she told DW of her upbringing in the occupied West Bank.

"I faced challenges in transportation. I wasn't able to go from one city to another to be able to train with other people, so that I can actually prepare for competitions. I needed to travel to other countries like Jordan or Egypt… which was very hard for me. And financially, the support wasn't really the support an elite athlete needed," she added.
Skepticism turns to sporting success
Growing up in Nablus, Bsharat had a narrow path to the top. But initially, it was her own reluctance that threatened to stop a champion career before it started.
"When I was a little kid, I did not really love it," Bsharat, who competes in the under-66 kilograms category, said.

"I started it because my family was in that sport. My father had a dojo and my mother also did that sport. My siblings and my aunts and my uncles, it's a family thing. I started it because they were all doing it. In time, I started getting into it."
How much power do Israeli settlers have over West Bank policy?

Family has been a constant source of comfort and inspiration for Bsharat. Her father and uncle have acted as manager and coach respectively. While her mother and siblings moved with Mariam to Hamburg, Germany, last year, her father remained in order to take care of his business, the dojo, though he visits and tries to be with his daughter in competitions. Integration has been made easier by her mastery of the language, taught to her by her German mother.
Nevertheless, Bsharat has mixed feelings about leaving her homeland.

"I'm thankful to be here because being in Germany opened lot of doors for me, and I think I have a brighter future here. But also being in Palestine was just my everyday life and I loved it there. My family was around me, my friends were around me, and I just felt comfortable, which was a big change coming here to Germany. I think every change comes with hardships."
Pressures from homeland weigh heavy

As well as the obvious difficulties of living in an area occupied by Israel, there are particular challenges for sportspeople living in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, with access to facilities, travel and constant security fears among them. As such, very few people from the Palestinian territories become successful on the international sporting stage. That, Bsharat said, gives her responsibilities that are unusual and heavy for a person of any age, let alone a 17-year-old.
Hamburg's refugee cricketers

"Being an elite athlete in Palestine is something very special because not everybody in Palestine has that opportunity. There aren't really a lot of athletes that are elite and who win international medals,” she said.

"So all that pressure from all the country and all the people, the family, the coaches are on me because I'm representing them, raising their flag. I sometimes even forget to fight for myself and actually think about myself."
Olympic dream alive but karate must find a way back

Remarkably that has not yet proved a barrier to Bsharat, who is is ranked first in the world in her category by the World Karate Federation (WKF). With Palestine recognized by the International Olympic Committee, Bsharat would likely have been a contender to raise that flag in Los Angeles at the 2028 Olympics. But the sport was dropped from the Games in 2024.

"The global karate community remains steadfast in our belief that the natural place for karate is within the Olympic Games, and we sincerely hope that the incongruence we suffered in Paris 2024 and LA 2028 will be corrected for Brisbane 2032, if not sooner," wrote the WKF in response to the decision in 2024. The sport was also taken off the slate for the recent Youth Games in Senegal.

Should the sport return in Brisbane, Bsharat would likely be approaching her prime. In the meantime, she is looking forward to starting her journey as a senior when she turns 18. But she won't be hanging around.
"My goal is it to be a world champion at seniors, which is the hardest and the best thing you can achieve in karate," she said.
"But winning an Olympic medal, being called Olympic champion or just representing my country with that flag [is a thought that] is just full of happiness and pride."
The interview was conducted by Janek Speight.
